newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Murder of S.Africa's Hani was tribute, says killer.
newsitem.headline: Murder of S.Africa's Hani was tribute, says killer.

text.p: The murder of South African communist leader Chris Hani was a tribute to how much he was loved, one of his far-right killers said on Wednesday.

Clive Derby-Lewis, applying for amnesty to the truth commission for the 1993 slaying, said only a man of Hani's great stature would do as a target for his scheme to plunge the country into chaos deep enough for a right-wing coup.
"Hani had to be the target. No one else had the following he had -- perhaps it can be seen as a tribute to Chris Hani that he was chosen," he said.
Only African National Congress (ANC) leader Nelson Mandela, three years out of jail and heavily protected, had a stronger following.
Hani's family is fiercely fighting his two killers' bid for amnesty, which the Truth and Reconciliation Commission can grant for political crimes whose perpetrators come clean.
Derby-Lewis, a former member of the all-white parliament, provided the gun from which his accomplice, Polish immigrant Janusz Walus, fired four bullets into Hani outside his home.
The Conservative Party politician gave details of the killing for the first time at the amnesty committee hearing in Pretoria.
He said he gave Walus an untraceable gun with a silencer but had not expected him to act so soon.

"It came as a terrible shock. Had something happened to come to our rescue so we wouldn't have to carry out our plan?" he said he had wondered when hearing news of the murder on the radio. But he heard the next day that Walus had been caught, and was arrested himself a week later.
The most prominent murder in modern South African history sent the country to the edge of the abyss -- as the plotters, sentenced to death and now serving life, had hoped.
Derby-Lewis said right-wing infighting scuppered their chance of seizing power.
Mandela and the National Party of then president F.W. de Klerk thwarted his aims by keeping years of peace talks on track and historic elections brought majority rule 12 months later.
The committee, which is considering amnesty for the murderers of American student Amy Biehl, is due to sit for another 10 days and rule later this year.
Hani's family lawyers hope to prove the applicants have not told all and cannot win their freedom.
